It’s also worth recalling some other similar incidents in the last few weeks.
On 18 October, an Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to ​Vienna diverted to Sofia ‌after a reported bomb ​threat while over Romania, Reuters said.
And yesterday, on 2 November, a WizzAir flight from London to Sofia was diverted to Budapest after a bomb threat (10:44).
Jakub Krupa
Reuters is carrying a quick confirmation that the flight from Bergamo to Sofia in Bulgaria was operated by WizzAir, not Ryanair.
This has also been updated in the tally at the top of the page.

There is also an update from Bulgaria, with the country’s transport ministry telling Reuters the bomb threats were actually made against two planes from Bergamo in Italy and Dublin in Ireland, and not from Israel as previously reported.
That brings the total to seven planes (that we know of).
Back to Berlin, Ukraine’s Zelenskyy also rejects Russia’s suggestion of a meeting in Moscow as “counterproductive.” He says what’s needed is serious talks, and not a gimmick.
He also insists that Russia has no advantage on the frontline at the moment.
Merz then adds that the 19 November meeting will decide further support for Ukraine in 2027, and that concludes the press.
Two false bomb threats reported on Italy-bound Ryanair flights

Meanwhile, two more false bomb threats were reported in Italy involving Ryanair flights from Lisbon and Dublin to Rome’s Fiumicino Airport, according to the Italian newspapers La Repubblica and Corriere della Sera.
The plane from Dublin was escorted by two Italian air force fighter jets, newspaper reported.
In both cases, routine checks were confirmed as negative, meaning no threat was identified, SkyTG24 said.
That brings the total of flights affected by false alarms today to at least six, up from four reported earlier (that we know of).
Security guarantees, Ukraine reconstructions, energy and Black Sea truce to be discussed in Abu Dhabi, Zelenskyy says

Asked about his expectations for the Abu Dhabi talks, Zelenskyy says he hopes to see future security guarantees for Ukraine to be covered, alongside a “prosperity package” that would help with the reconstruction of Ukraine.
He also says he hopes to discuss a proposal on energy, Black Sea truce, which is “in the interest of not only Ukraine, but also Russia and various nations in Africa.”
He reiterates that “there can be no stable peace unless Europe is at the negotiating table.”
Merz for his part says that “it is crucial for Russia to finally engage in serious negotiations.”
Europe remains 'crucial' for ending the war in Ukraine, Zelenskyy says, as he confirms Abu Dhabi talks

Responding, Zelenskyy thanks Germany for its continued help, including on air defence, and says that while many people will be following the events in the US today’s midterm elections, “the role of Europe – and specifically Germany – remains crucial.”
He says he briefed Merz on the latest attacks on Ukraine.
He also confirms the upcoming Abu Dhabi talks on 10-11 November (11:21), which he says hopefully “will pave the way for a trilateral meeting at the level of heads of states and government.”

He also confirms further talks on Ukraine will be held in Brussels on Wednesday (12:41), as per the European Commission’s announcement earlier, and that the coalition of the willing will meet in Berlin on 19 November.
Merz declares Germany will keep supporting Ukraine as he warns about Russia's attacks, impact of Black Sea strikes on food security
Germany’s Merz begins by saying Zelenskyy’s visit comes “at a critical moment” as Russian attacks on Ukraine continued with “undiminished – indeed, increasing – severity and ruthlessness.”
He says Ukraine “can continue to rely on Germany,” with more support from Berlin in the coming months, including on air defence, energy, and broader winter-related aid.
Merz also warns that the outcome of the war in Ukraine “will determine European security for a long time to come.”
He says Germany will be coordinating with France and the UK, and will host a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin later this month.

The German chancellor also talks of growing concerns about the broader effects of the continuing war, including a potential “global food crisis” triggered by Russia’s continued attacks on trading routes in the Black Sea.
He says the upcoming Abu Dhabi talks are “the right step forward,” and Europe hopes to play its part.
In the meantime, Berlin and partners will “increase the pressure on Moscow and continue to support Ukraine,” he says.
Meanwhile, Germany’s Merz and Ukraine’s Zelenskyy are now briefing the media after their talks in Berlin.
I will bring you the key lines here.
Polish authorities call off bomb alert on London flight
Similarly, Warsaw-Modlin Airport has also given the all-clear after concluding security sweeps on a LOT Polish Airlines flight from London Heathrow following an earlier bomb alert (10:33).
The airport said:
“The bomb threat was called off … Following the completion of operations by the relevant services, Warsaw/Modlin Airport has returned to normal functioning.”
Spanish police rules out presence of explosives on Ryanair flight to Murcia
We have just got an update from Spain’s Guardia Civil on the Ryanair flight from Manchester to Murcia (12:44).
The authorities “ruled out the presence of explosives on the plane,” the Spanish government’s delegate in the region of Murcia, Francisco Lucas, confirmed.
“The International Airport of the Region of Murcia resumes its activity normally. Thanks to the emergency teams that have participated in the operation,” he said.
Swedish centrist Thand Ringqvist rejected as prime minister as search for new government continues
Over in Sweden, centrist leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist has just lost a vote on her proposed government – which is hardly surprising given that even she as very clear she had no chance of winning.
324 votes against, 25 in favour.
It’s been 51 days since the Swedish parliamentary election, and it’s the second failed attempt to form the government. Two more and we get a snap election. Gulp.

The next attempt is expected to be led by the interim centre-right prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, but his outgoing coalition is also unlikely to secure enough support in the parliament, further complicating the process.
Here are some more photos from Berlin where Zelenskyy is now taking part in talks with Merz (11:53).
Flights from London, Copenhagen, Manchester and Israel affected by bomb threats

If you are joining us now, we are following reports about at least four planes affected by bomb threats across Europe this morning: two in Poland (from the UK 10:33, 10:58, 12:00 and Denmark 11:33, 12:59), one in Bulgaria (from Israel 12:50), and one in Spain (from the UK 12:44).

All four of them landed safely and are being checked by security services. It may be nothing, but is highly unusual (particularly after another alert yesterday 10:44), so we are keeping a close eye on that.

Separately, we are keeping an eye on Berlin where Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy is just arriving to meet German chancellor Friedrich Merz on his previously unannounced high-security trip to Berlin.
We should hear from them in the next hour or so.
The Scandinavian SAS airline has issued a brief statement confirming its earlier incident in Warsaw (11:33).

Note, that’s two separate incidents involving two separate flights in Warsaw – a PLL LOT flight from London Heathrow to Warsaw-Okęcie, diverted to Warsaw-Modlin (10:33, 10:58, 12:00), and a SAS flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Okęcie.
The airline said:

“We can confirm that a threat has been made against flight SK751 between Copenhagen and Warsaw. The aircraft landed normally in Warsaw and the passengers have disembarked. We are following established security procedures while taking care of our passengers and crew. The matter is now being handled by the police in Warsaw, and we are following their instructions. We refer any further questions regarding the threat to the relevant authorities and the police in Warsaw.”
And Reuters is reporting a fourth plane affected by a bomb threat this morning, this time in Bulgaria.

A plane flying ⁠from ⁠Israel landed at ​Sofia airport after ⁠a bomb threat was ⁠received ​by email, Reuters reported after local media, with counter-terrorism units deployed to check for possible explosive devices.
The airport’s website shows only one plane from Israel landing there this morning: an El Al service from Tel Aviv.
Bulgarian public broadcaster BNT reported that it was a part of a broader bomb threat alert, affecting “various institutions.”
Meanwhile, we are getting news about a third bomb threat issued against a plane in Europe this morning: this time it’s a Ryanair flight FR4116 from Manchester to Murcia in Spain.
The plane landed safely at Murcia airport. 114 passengers and 7 crew members safely disembarked the plane which is now being checked by security services.
The report was confirmed by the Spanish government’s delegate in the region of Murcia, Francisco Lucas, and reported by local media.
EU to host talks on Ukraine with EU, US, Nato, World Bank on Wednesday

The European Commission will host ⁠a meeting regarding Ukraine with representatives ⁠from the ⁠United ​States, Ukraine and its key European allies on Wednesday, Commission ⁠spokesperson Paula Pinho said.

“So tomorrow the European ⁠Commission will host a ​meeting with representatives ‌from Ukraine, ‌from the United States, France, Germany, ‌the UK, Nato and the World Bank and this meeting will build on earlier talks that took place ‌in Miami,” Pinho told reporters in Brussels.
United States’ envoy ​Steve Witkoff had said earlier that this meeting would take place in Brussels, Reuters added.

items.titel: Czech public broadcasters hold historic strike following government vote to abolish license fees
items.anriss: A strike by workers of public TV and radio workers interrupted broadcasts and drew thousands of people onto the streets across the Czech Republic.

absaetze.t: First published in Deník N.
A strike by workers of public TV and radio workers interrupted broadcasts and drew thousands of people onto the streets across the Czech Republic.
Thousands of protesters gathered in Prague, Brno and Ostrava demonstrations supported by media, students, theatres and more than 300 Czech athletes.

“An unprecedented day in the history of Czech public service media has begun”, said Michal Kubal, Czech Television’s news chief, at 00:00 on 3 November 2026 marking a start to an all-day strike by the broadcasting workers.

He read an opening statement from a sheet of paper during the midnight dispatch. “This broadcast will change. The midnight news is one of many programmes that will look completely different on Czech Television screens from what viewers are used to,” Daniel Stach said on air. The organiser of the strike appeared on TV with a darkened studio as backdrop.

Presenter Kubal went on to explain that staff at Czech Television and Czech Radio were using the one-day strike to fight for independence of both public service media outlets, in response to a government moves to scrap license fees and move public their funding to the state budget.
TV management had concluded a memorandum with the strike organisers under which media staff would provide essential news coverage in the event of extraordinary developments.

"A large majority of women and men working at both media outlets have joined the strike. This afternoon, they will also take part in public gatherings in Prague and other cities in support of public service media," Kubal added.
Those tuning into ČT24 could see a notice about the the public broadcaster's news network minimalist provisional regime.

"Czech Television employees are on strike. We are doing everything we can to ensure that we can continue providing a public service in full and to the highest standard in the future," the notice read.
A STEM/MARK survey for Czech Television says 68 percent of people of Czechs agree public service media should stay well away from state control or private ownership.

"Thank you for watching Czech Television — in times of crisis, at historically pivotal moments and on entirely ordinary weekdays," said Stach, one of the leading figures of the Veřejnoprávně initiative, which called the strike, as he concluded the roughly five-minute midnight news bulletin.

items.titel: La France a besoin d’une révolution bureaucratique. L’IA pourrait la rendre possible
items.anriss: Le 29 septembre dernier, Donald Trump a inauguré America.gov, un portail permettant de poser une question en langage courant (comment renouveler un passeport, comment s’inscrire à Medicare) et d’obtenir une réponse puisée dans 29 000 sites …

absaetze.t: Testez le Grand Continent. Les idées et les analyses qu’on ne trouve nulle part. Mais que vous verrez bientôt partout. Dans votre boîte mail à partir de 8 euros par mois

Le 29 septembre dernier, Donald Trump a inauguré America.gov, un portail permettant de poser une question en langage courant (comment renouveler un passeport, comment s’inscrire à Medicare) et d’obtenir une réponse puisée dans 29 000 sites fédéraux. Le site a été conçu sous la direction de Joe Gebbia, cofondateur d’Airbnb et administrateur de Tesla. Sa première mission au sein du Département de l’efficacité gouvernementale (DOGE) consistait à numériser les départs à la retraite des fonctionnaires fédéraux, au moment où l’administration les poussait vers la sortie. Lors du lancement d’America.gov, Donald Trump a aussi remercié Edward Coristine, 20 ans, connu au DOGE sous le surnom de « Big Balls ». Le site fonctionne avec Gemini, le modèle de Google, et avec Grok, celui d’Elon Musk. Un décret présidentiel somme les agences fédérales de s’y raccorder au plus vite 1. La porte d’entrée numérique de la première puissance mondiale porte ainsi la signature de l’administration qui a fait de la tronçonneuse un programme de gouvernement.

Alors qu’en France et en Europe, l’État démocratique 2 est attaqué pour sa lenteur et sa lourdeur, l’intelligence artificielle ouvre des possibilités que le numérique seul ne permettait pas : décloisonner les silos administratifs, passer d’une posture de guichet à une logique proactive, organiser des boucles de rétroaction permanentes avec les usagers et les citoyens.
Le même outil peut aussi exposer des données personnelles, faciliter la surveillance et créer des dépendances à des acteurs privés, dont la puissance rivalise désormais avec celle des États.
Mais le statu quo n’offre aucune garantie de sécurité ni de qualité : il prolonge la complexité des parcours administratifs et les dépendances technologiques existantes.

La France pourrait se donner une ambition immense : devenir, avec ses partenaires européens, la référence mondiale d’un gouvernement démocratique à l’ère de l’IA agentique. Faire la démonstration, par la qualité du service rendu et par la protection effective des droits, que l’Europe sait développer et maîtriser des technologies de pointe et en faire bénéficier ses citoyens, tout en restant fidèle à ses principes démocratiques.
« Bonjour, État » n’est plus de la science-fiction
Les évolutions technologiques récentes permettent d’envisager la création d’un assistant public numérique complet et ambitieux – appelons-le « Bonjour, État » 3 .

Cet outil serait capable de répondre aux questions de la vie réelle (« Bonjour État, je viens de perdre mon emploi, quels sont mes droits ? », « Ma mère entre en dépendance, par où commencer ? », « J’ai un projet de petite entreprise, quelles démarches ? »), de préremplir les dossiers correspondants, d’orienter vers le bon interlocuteur humain quand la situation le requiert et de faire remonter en temps réel les incompréhensions récurrentes et les points de friction, afin qu’ils déclenchent une révision des règles ou des interfaces concernées.
Cette ambition peut sembler lointaine. Pourtant, les premières briques d’un tel gouvernement agentique existent déjà et se déploient rapidement.

Le premier niveau est l’assistant informatif, d’ores et déjà proposé par des institutions publiques et des entreprises privées. GOV.UK Chat au Royaume-Uni et Gov.pt au Portugal permettent d’interroger, à l’écrit ou oralement, de vastes ensembles d’informations administratives dans une interface unique et de répondre aux questions des citoyens à partir des informations officielles. L’Estonie déploie également Bürokratt, un réseau d’assistants destiné à faciliter l’accès aux différentes administrations. Côté privé, Polimorphic et CivicPlus commercialisent auprès des collectivités américaines des assistants capables de répondre aux questions des habitants.

Le deuxième niveau est le guichet transactionnel, qui sait instruire et accomplir certaines démarches. Diia.AI en Ukraine et TAMM à Abou Dhabi permettent déjà de réaliser certaines opérations administratives par la conversation : obtenir un certificat de revenus ou de résidence, renouveler une licence ou régler certaines factures.

Le troisième et dernier niveau serait l’assistant-compagnon, qui suit le citoyen au fil des événements de vie (entrée dans la vie d’adulte, changement d’orientation professionnelle, naissance, etc.), mobilise les services concernés, conserve le contexte des échanges et peut prendre des initiatives sous le contrôle de l’usager.

Imaginons un citoyen qui perd son emploi. Son assistant pourrait identifier ses droits à indemnisation, préparer les démarches auprès de France Travail, vérifier son éligibilité à d’autres prestations, lui proposer des formations adaptées et assurer le suivi de l’ensemble, sans qu’il ait à répéter sa situation à chaque administration.

Les silos séparent aussi les échelons territoriaux. La cantine de l’école relève de la commune, celle du collège du département, celle du lycée de la région, et chacune a ses propres tarifs, ses propres règles. Une famille dont les enfants vont à l’école, au collège et au lycée jongle donc avec trois factures et souvent trois portails. Sans même toucher aux compétences des collectivités, « Bonjour, État » pourrait se connecter aux différents portails, effectuer les démarches et présenter les trois factures de manière homogène.

Plusieurs acteurs travaillent déjà sur les capacités nécessaires : TAMM organise ses services autour des événements de vie et automatise certaines tâches récurrentes ; ServiceNow développe l’orchestration de procédures entre administrations ; le Royaume-Uni prépare avec Anthropic un assistant personnel destiné, dans un premier temps, à accompagner les demandeurs d’emploi. Mais leur intégration dans un service universel suppose encore un travail important sur les données, les systèmes informatiques, les processus et les responsabilités.
Le coût de l’inaction

Les bénéfices d’un « Bonjour, État » sont potentiellement considérables : recul massif de la complexité bureaucratique et donc du non-recours aux droits, augmentation de la satisfaction des usagers, amélioration continue des services grâce à la prise en compte permanente des retours des citoyens. L’IA pourrait aussi libérer les agents publics d’une partie des tâches administratives répétitives et leur redonner du temps pour exercer leur cœur de métier.

Les risques sont évidents : perte d’autonomie et déqualification des agents publics, atteinte à la vie privée, dérive autoritaire facilitée par l’outil technologique. L’automatisation pourrait également reproduire, voire amplifier, les erreurs et les discriminations existantes, tout en rendant plus difficile l’identification des responsabilités. Les contrôles automatisés sont ainsi régulièrement pointés du doigt. Aux Pays-Bas, l’utilisation de profils de risque algorithmiques a contribué à un système de contrôle discriminatoire des allocations de garde d’enfants, qui a injustement mis en cause des dizaines de milliers de familles. Le troisième gouvernement Rutte a démissionné en janvier 2021 en partie à la suite de ce scandale 4. En Australie, le recouvrement automatisé de trop-perçus, dit Robodebt, a été jugé illégal dès 2019, avant de faire l’objet d’un rapport accablant d’une commission royale en 2023 5.

Dans ce contexte, la tentation est forte de vouloir ralentir, de souhaiter une forme de moratoire de l’usage de l’IA dans les administrations. Plusieurs voix se sont d’ores et déjà élevées dans ce sens. Ces inquiétudes sont légitimes, et les déboires de la dématérialisation administrative invitent à la prudence. En 2017, la bascule en ligne des cartes grises a ainsi laissé des usagers des mois sans titre et fait prospérer des sites privés qui facturaient des frais pour une démarche gratuite sur le site officiel 6.
Mais à trop redouter Orwell, on se résigne à Kafka. Il faut mesurer les conséquences d’un non-choix.

L’État démocratique européen est fragilisé dans son modèle. Il est devenu incapable d’organiser à l’échelle et systématiquement des relations de qualité avec ses usagers, qu’ils soient particuliers ou entreprises, de fournir des services publics de grande qualité sur l’ensemble de son territoire et de relever les défis des transitions climatique et technologique. 61 % des Français déclarent ainsi rencontrer parfois ou souvent des difficultés dans leurs démarches administratives 7. 43 % des Français approuvent l’idée qu’il faudrait « moins de démocratie et plus d’efficacité » 8.

Le sentiment d’inefficacité est exacerbé par la comparaison avec le secteur privé. Les usagers attendent désormais des services plus personnalisés, plus souples, plus faciles d’accès, comme ceux que proposent les plateformes privées en matière de services financiers, de commerce en ligne, de préparation de voyage, etc. Ces comparaisons sont en partie injustes, car l’État ne choisit pas ses usagers, ne sélectionne pas ses missions, ne peut pas refuser un dossier complexe. Mais elles ne peuvent être écartées d’un revers de main , car l’opinion que chacun se fait de l’État se forge d’abord dans ses interactions quotidiennes avec les administrations.

Le statu quo comporte également ses propres risques technologiques. La vétusté et la fragmentation de certains systèmes informatiques compliquent leur maintenance et leur sécurisation. Les agents utilisent déjà, parfois sans cadre adapté, des outils d’intelligence artificielle. Une transformation agentique mal conçue pourrait certes multiplier les points d’accès sensibles et les vulnérabilités ; mais ne rien faire ne protège pas davantage les administrations contre les cyberattaques ou les défaillances de service. Un programme ambitieux serait ainsi l’occasion de moderniser les systèmes, de maîtriser les accès et de reconstituer des compétences technologiques publiques.

L’inaction ne ferait qu’accélérer la défiance vis-à-vis de la puissance publique, et encourager ceux qui souhaitent la démanteler ou la réduire à son appareil sécuritaire. Elle laisserait aussi les entreprises privées développer leurs propres assistants administratifs, capables demain de renseigner les citoyens, de connaître leur situation personnelle et d’agir pour leur compte. Le mouvement est engagé. Aux États-Unis, HelloGov, qui vient de fusionner avec le spécialiste des visas iVisa, prépare passeports et visas pour le compte des particuliers, moyennant des frais. La société a également lancé GovSchema, un projet de standard ouvert destiné à rendre les procédures administratives directement lisibles par des agents IA. Même ouvert, ce standard est né de l’initiative d’un acteur marchand, faute d’État pour le prendre. C’est cet acteur qui commence à écrire la grammaire des futures interactions entre les machines et l’État 9. Les cartes grises l’ont montré à petite échelle : là où l’État est défaillant, des intermédiaires marchands occupent le terrain, sans les mêmes garanties de transparence et de confidentialité. La porte d’entrée vers les services publics pourrait ainsi échapper progressivement aux administrations elles-mêmes.

Cette intermédiation n’est pourtant que le premier degré de la dépossession. Le second, plus grave, intervient lorsque des entreprises technologiques s’installent au cœur des administrations, prennent la main sur les données et orientent les décisions. Aux États-Unis, ICE, la police fédérale de l’immigration, s’appuie sur Palantir pour piloter ses opérations. En avril 2025, l’agence lui a commandé, pour 30 millions de dollars, une plateforme de suivi des migrants en temps réel. Les logiciels de cette même entreprise équipent le Pentagone et plusieurs agences fédérales de santé.

items.titel: Zelensky dit espérer que les discussions sous médiation américaine aboutiront à une rencontre avec Poutine
items.anriss: Le président ukrainien était ce mardi 3 novembre à Berlin. Volodomyr Zelensky a participé à une conférence sur la sécurité et rencontré le chancelier Merz. Les deux responsables ont évoqué les prochains rendez-vous diplomatiques pour …

absaetze.t: Le président ukrainien était ce mardi 3 novembre à Berlin. Volodomyr Zelensky a participé à une conférence sur la sécurité et rencontré le chancelier Merz. Les deux responsables ont évoqué les prochains rendez-vous diplomatiques pour tenter de trouver une issue à la guerre. Ils ont insisté sur le rôle essentiel de l'Europe dans cette perspective.
1 min Temps de lecture
Avec notre correspondant à Berlin, Pascal Thibaut

Pendant que les Américains se rendaient aux urnes, Volodymyr Zelensky à Berlin remerciait à nouveau les États-Unis pour leur soutien passé. Mais la énième visite du président ukrainien à Berlin, principal soutien de Kiev, a mis surtout en exergue le rôle de l’Allemagne et, au-delà, des Européens. Volodymyr Zelensky a espéré que les prochains pourparlers à Abou Dhabi débouchent sur une rencontre avec Vladimir Poutine.

« Nous espérons que le format des réunions tripartites entre l'Ukraine, les États-Unis et la Russie reprendra prochainement, du 10 au 12 novembre. C’est précisément ce format, au niveau des dirigeants, qui permettra de résoudre les questions clés pour parvenir à une paix durable », a-t-il déclaré.

Volodymyr Zelensky a estimé que les questions prioritaires pour cette rencontre devaient être l’énergie avec un cessez-le-feu de part et d’autre, le déblocage de la mer Noire pour l’exportation de céréales, mais aussi l’augmentation des échanges de prisonniers.

Dans deux semaines, le président ukrainien sera à nouveau à Berlin pour une rencontre de la « coalition des volontaires » avec de nombreux chefs d’État et de gouvernement. Friedrich Merz a annoncé une aide de son pays de 200 millions d’euros pour aider l’Ukraine à surmonter l’hiver qui approche. Le chancelier a rappelé que tous les Européens, et non seulement l’Allemagne, doivent assumer leur responsabilité pour répondre aux engagements pris au sein de l’Otan pour soutenir l’Ukraine.

items.titel: Italy holds emergency talks as supermarket fridge attacks spread across Europe
items.anriss: The EU says the cyberattacks are a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain, but Romania’s cyber chief calls them “semi-amateurish”.

absaetze.t: Published on 3 November 2026 - 21:22 GMT+1
Italy’s government held emergency talks with intelligence chiefs on Tuesday after cyberattacks on supermarket freezer systems hit at least 11 European countries in recent days.
ADVERTISEMENT

Supermarkets in at least 10 EU countries, including Germany, Italy and the Netherlands, have been forced to throw away food after temperatures rose in their fridges and freezers. The UK has also been affected.
Nobody has claimed responsibility and the motive remains unknown.
The Italian government said the impact so far was “highly limited”, and that only outlets with outdated security systems had been affected. Around 20 stores were reported hit nationwide.
Ministers nevertheless met intelligence chiefs and Italy’s National Cyber Security Agency, which issued technical advice to retailers on protecting their systems.

Giuseppe Spadaro, director of a group that runs Coop supermarkets in Sicily, said four of its 300 stores had been hit. “We had to throw away everything. The shelves are empty,” he told the Corriere della Sera newspaper.

EU spokesperson Thomas Regnier said EU agencies were working with national authorities on a collective response. “These are not isolated incidents, and of course, we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents,” he said.
On Monday, EU food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen called the attacks a “deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain”.

Romania’s cybersecurity chief took a different view. Six Romanian outlets were affected, but Dan Cimpean, director of the country’s National Cyber Security Directorate, said: “It seems semi-amateurish. We do not suspect, under any circumstances, that it is a state actor.”

In the UK, National Cyber Security Centre chief Richard Horne told the BBC the issue affected “the whole food supply chain”, and that there had been a couple of instances where “vulnerable technology had been exploited”.
Four stores were hit in Germany. In Sweden, the Coop chain said its seven affected shops were back to normal, and that the equipment involved had been connected over old 4G mobile networks.
Belgium was among the hardest-hit countries, and federal prosecutors there have opened an investigation. Hundreds of French supermarkets were hit by a similar attack last month.

Supermarket refrigeration systems are often connected to the internet so that contractors can monitor and repair them remotely. Recent research by the security firm Forescout found nearly 13,000 refrigeration control services openly reachable online in 99 countries

items.titel: Tausende protestieren gegen tschechische Rundfunk-Pläne
items.anriss: Tschechiens Regierung will den öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunk künftig aus dem Staatshaushalt finanzieren. Viele sorgen sich deshalb um die Unabhängigkeit der Sender. Tausende gingen auf die Straße, beim Rundfunk wurde gestreikt.[ mehr ]

absaetze.t: Tschechiens Regierung will den öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunk künftig aus dem Staatshaushalt finanzieren. Viele sorgen sich deshalb um die Unabhängigkeit der Sender. Tausende gingen auf die Straße, beim Rundfunk wurde gestreikt.

In Prag und anderen tschechischen Städten haben erneut Tausende Menschen gegen Pläne der Regierung demonstriert, die Finanzierung der öffentlich-rechtlichen Sender zu ändern und zu kürzen. Mitarbeiter des tschechischen Fernsehens und Radios traten in einen Streik, um gegen das Gesetzesvorhaben von Regierungschef Andrej Babis zu protestieren. Das tschechische Fernsehen und das tschechische Radio mussten ihr Programm einschränken. Der 24-Stunden-Nachrichtensender des Fernsehens zeigte einen verdunkelten Newsroom und Moderatoren in schwarzer Kleidung.

In Prag zog die Menge von den Medienhäusern zum zentralen Wenzelsplatz, wo sich Studierende und weitere Demonstrierende dem Protest anschlossen. Sie bezeichnen die Pläne als Versuch, die Unabhängigkeit der Sender zu untergraben. "Ich möchte, dass die Medien weiterhin frei sind", sagte eine junge Studentin der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters. Viele trugen dreieckige Papierhüte, die einer beliebten Zeichentrickfigur des tschechischen Fernsehens ähneln und zu einem Symbol der Proteste geworden sind.
Direkte Zuwendung statt Rundfunkgebühr

Ende Oktober hatte das tschechische Abgeordnetenhaus das umstrittene Gesetz im Schnellverfahren in erster Lesung abgesegnet. Die Vorlage muss nun noch die zweite Parlamentskammer, den Senat, passieren, bevor sie dem Staatschef zur Unterschrift vorgelegt werden kann.

Statt über von den Bürgern gezahlte Rundfunkgebühren sollen sich das öffentlich-rechtliche Radio und Fernsehen künftig durch direkte staatliche Zuwendungen finanzieren. Dies dürfte für die Sender eine Budgetkürzung um 15 Prozent im kommenden Jahr bedeuten. Die Regierung verlangt von den Sendern Einsparungen und versichert zugleich, dass das neue Finanzierungsmodell ihre redaktionelle Unabhängigkeit und ihre Programminhalte nicht beeinträchtige.
Vorbilder Orban und Fico?

Babis führt ein Regierungsbündnis, dem zwei Rechtsaußen-Parteien angehören. Die Koalition wirft den öffentlich-rechtlichen Medien vor, parteiisch zu sein. Bei ihrer Amtseinführung im Dezember hatte die Regierung daher eine Reform des öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunks angekündigt.

Kritiker, darunter die Europäische Rundfunkunion (EBU), die Europäische Journalisten-Föderation sowie die Organisation Reporter ohne Grenzen, werfen Babis vor, dass Finanzierungsentscheidungen durch die Reform politischem Druck ausgesetzt würden. - nach dem Vorbild des slowakischen Ministerpräsidenten Robert Fico und des ehemaligen ungarischen Regierungschefs Viktor Orban.

"Dieser Vorschlag, sollte er verabschiedet werden, wird der Regierungskoalition Werkzeuge an die Hand geben, um den Inhalt beider öffentlicher Medien politisch zu beeinflussen", sagte Jan Molacek, Reporter beim tschechischen Fernsehen, der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters. Eine von den Sendern als untragbar bezeichnete Kürzung von 15 Prozent würde die Budgets auf das Niveau von vor rund 20 Jahren drücken.

items.titel: French government launches fertility awareness campaign targeting 29-year-olds
items.anriss: The health insurance system is about to send 29-year-old men and women a message on fertility issues, a key measure in the government’s anti-infertility plan launched in February.

absaetze.t: Published on 3 November 2026 - 20:22 GMT+1

A report from the monitoring committee for the fertility plan was submitted on Tuesday 3 November to the health minister, Stéphanie Rist. Immediately afterwards, she announced the launch of a major information campaign to support all couples who are planning to have children.
ADVERTISEMENT

By the end of November, women and men in France aged 29 will receive an awareness letter from Assurance Maladie in order to "give every adult the means to understand and preserve their fertility", the minister said.

The letter will invite people who wish to have children to consult a health professional for "a preconception consultation", to review their health, lifestyle habits and any concerns "so as to prepare a future pregnancy as well as possible".

For couples who are trying to have a child but are not succeeding, the letter recommends consulting a specialised health professional, where there is no particular problem, after "one year of trying before the age of 35" and after "six months of trying after the age of 35".
While age is a decisive factor, fertility also depends on many medical, environmental and behavioural factors, including diet, sleep, physical activity and the consumption of tobacco and alcohol.

At the same time, the government says it is rolling out the "Ma fertilité" portal, which brings together a set of dedicated information on the Santé.fr website, as well as audio messages and posters in doctors' waiting rooms.
Towards an increase in the number of centres able to provide egg freezing

The novelty of this information campaign is relative, since it corresponds to one of the 16 measures in the plan against infertility presented last February by Stéphanie Rist, following the call for "demographic rearmament" launched by President Emmanuel Macron in 2024.

"In France, 15 to 25% of couples who wish to conceive a child encounter difficulties, that is more than three million people", the health minister recalled. She wants to increase the number of centres able to provide egg self-preservation for non-medical reasons.

The information letter that is about to be sent out recalls that in France, "it is possible to self-preserve one's gametes" (male or female reproductive cells) in view of a possible parenthood project.

Oocytes (female reproductive cells) can be collected and stored for women "between 29 and 37, for possible use up to the age of 45". For men, sperm can be stored "between 29 and 45, for possible use up to the age of 59".

Last year, more than 20,000 women asked to store their oocytes with a view to a future child. That is an increase of 30% in one year. But waiting times vary from 14 to 24 months depending on the region.

"Fertility is a major public health issue that concerns both women and men. Too often, difficulties are discovered late, whereas we can act earlier to better inform, prevent and support", the health minister wrote in her statement.

items.titel: Air Force divests its few A-29s, explores ‘future options’
items.anriss: A set of three A-29 Super Tucanos are destined for storage after officials at the Air Force Test Pilot School opted against using the turboprops, a spokesperson for Edwards Air Force Base told Breaking Defense.

absaetze.t: PARIS — The US Air Force is no longer planning to use three A-29 Super Tucanos for flight testing, opting instead to divest the service’s only examples of the Embraer-made turboprops.
“The A-29 Super Tucano was thoroughly evaluated but did not meet the intended use for Air Force Test Pilot School,” a spokesperson for Edwards Air Force Base said in a statement to Breaking Defense.

Those aircraft have now been “divested,” the spokesperson said, adding that officials “are exploring future options for a sustainable spin and mission systems aircraft” for the test pilot school. Aviation Week previously reported the Air Force’s decision to retire the aircraft.

The three A-29s were originally bought by Air Force Special Operations Command, but the command off-loaded the aircraft “after mission requirements changed,” the Air Force said in a 2024 release. The test pilot school at Edwards then picked up the turboprop trio to see if it could fill various test school needs.

Brazilian aerospace company Embraer manufactures the A-29 and assembles the aircraft at an assembly line in Jacksonville, Fla., where US firm SNC subsequently installs mission equipment for the US and specific foreign military sales customers. Embraer officials have said the Jacksonville line could be at risk if sufficient demand does not materialize, though the company also runs a separate Super Tucano production facility in Brazil.
The fate of Edwards’ A-29 fleet was previously revealed in a notice posted by the Air Force Oct. 29, which said the service plans to sole-source a contract with SNC to safely store the aircraft.

“These aircraft are not expected to return to flight for use by the Air Force,” the notice says. The contract to store them would come with a single base year and options for an additional two years of work.
SNC and Embraer did not respond to a request for comment by press time.

The US Air Force itself never bought the A-29 in significant numbers, but the service did acquire the aircraft for allies like the Afghan armed forces prior to the Taliban takeover. In recent years, the growing threat of unmanned systems has prompted Embraer and SNC to pitch the Super Tucano as a more affordable drone killer.

items.titel: US Air Force asks industry for new cruise missile for Ukraine
items.anriss: The U.S. Air Force is asking the defense industry whether it can deliver a new cruise missile intended for Ukraine.

absaetze.t: The U.S. Air Force is asking the defense industry whether it can deliver a new cruise missile intended for Ukraine.
Potential contractors are asked to detail their capabilities to provide the Extended Range Attack Munition, a small, air-launched standoff missile intended for mass production.

The Air Force’s new Request For Information, which has a deadline of Nov. 19, offers some technical specifications for ERAM. It should be a 500-pound class weapon with a range of greater than 250 nautical miles and a speed of more than Mach 0.6. Terminal accuracy should be within 10 meters of the target even amid jamming, such as degraded GPS. In addition to blast and fragmentation effects, the weapon should also be capable of limited penetration on impact.

The Air Force describes ERAM as a next-generation cruise missile “designed to provide affordable mass to the fight,” and which “delivers a precision-guided, stand-off capability against high-value fixed targets.”

ERAM is part of the Pentagon’s push for cheaper weapons developed more quickly. In 2024, the Air Force awarded a contract to two small defense companies — Zone 5 Technologies and CoAspire — to develop ERAM prototypes. In January 2026 — less than a year and a half later, the Air Force conducted a live warhead test at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida.

Similar haste can be seen in the RFI, which states that companies should begin delivering the first of more than 1,000 ERAMs no later than three months after the contract is awarded. Deliveries should be complete within 15 months.

One question is whether Ukraine is already using ERAM on its American-made F-16 fighters. In August 2025, the Trump administration announced an $825 million sale of 3,350 ERAMs to Ukraine. In June 2026, Ukrainian media suggested that Ukraine has used the AGM-188A Rusty Dagger — an ERAM version — against the Voronezh Semiconductor Plant, which makes components for Russian missiles.

Another question is to what extent the U.S. military will make use of ERAM. The Air Force published the original RFI in January 2024, nearly two years into the Ukraine War — and nearly two years before the Iran war depleted U.S. inventories of expensive missiles.

items.titel: The Indian Pavilion in Venice Asks: What Is Home?
items.anriss: VENICE – The Indian Pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale is to visual art what minor tones are to music: striking notes that invite contemplation and convey depth. Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home interprets the Biennale’s theme, …

absaetze.t: "Geographies of Distance" offers a polysemous reading of home during a period of accelerated urbanization in India.
November 3, 2026 — 4 min read

VENICE — The Indian Pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale is to visual art what minor tones are to music: striking notes that invite contemplation and convey depth. Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home interprets the Biennale’s theme, “In Minor Keys,” through the rich diversity encompassed by India's name. The exhibition offers a polysemous reading of home in a country where time and space are measured on a vast scale, bringing together disparate experiences of place, memory, distance, and belonging.

The exhibition represents all of India: from the sun-baked earth of the southern state of Tamil Nadu to the stepped architecture of Ladakh in the north, to houses at the foot of the Himalayas, and to the ghost of a Delhi long succumbing to bulldozers. Enormous flowers hang from the ceiling, standing in for gardens and their most distinctive inhabitants, a tribute to their prominent place in Indian private, public, and sacred life. A mesh of bamboo canes evokes a widespread construction technique in the East, symbolizing new cities rising above older urban landscapes.

“I would characterize the pavilion and the work of the five artists as a reflection on identity and belonging in a period of accelerated change,” said Amin Jaffer, curator of Geographies of Distance. “[It] proposes the idea that home is not solely a physical place we inhabit but a condition that we carry with us.”

absaetze.t: Paul Ramírez Jonas debuted his participatory artwork “Public Trust” months before Trump was first elected. A decade on, it feels more urgent than ever.
November 3, 2026 — 4 min read

Last month, Paul Ramírez Jonas invited the people of Toronto to sit down with a stranger in a public space, make a promise, swear on it, see it spelled out on a large-scale marquee, and then memorialize it in a one-of-a-kind contract they kept. One of hundreds of such vows was: “I promise to disagree better.”

Ramírez Jonas’s participatory public artwork “Public Trust,” presented by The Bentway (where Anna Gallagher-Ross directs programming), was commissioned and first showcased by Now + There (founded by Kate Gilbert and later renamed the Boston Public Art Triennial) in 2016, months before Donald Trump was elected as president.

“Public Trust” was the Now + There’s first project, a labor of love for its one-and-a-half-person team, and has since set the standard for its commissions. The promises made by everyday Bostonians — often similar in their commitments to family or self-improvement but coming from very different walks of life — were juxtaposed with daily headlines, including promises by politicians, corporations, weather forecasters, and more. This intermingling of commitments, both personal and authoritative, invites us to reflect on the power of our words, participation, and role in the democratic process. Ramírez Jonas often quips that he would like this project to one day become irrelevant.

Ten years later, in the lead-up to our municipal election in Toronto, we could think of no better project to invite people to reflect on the power of their words and their participation. Why does the simple act of sitting across from a stranger and making a promise feel more important than ever?
Opinion
Paul Ramirez Jonas
Boston

items.titel: New York Studio School revamp unearths long-forgotten murals
items.anriss: A renovation project at the historic building—the original home of the Whitney Museum of American Art—has uncovered works by Robert E. Locher and Cecily Brown

absaetze.t: Back in 1907, Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney established her sculpture studio in a converted stable and hayloft on MacDougal Alley in the heart of Manhattan’s Greenwich Village. The heiress and artist then proceeded to procure four neighbouring brownstones one by one, with the Lincoln Memorial sculptor Daniel Chester French being the last holdout.

The five buildings that now comprise 8 West 8th Street are some of the New York art world’s most storied. It was here that Whitney promoted US artists at a time when they were widely denigrated, and where she opened the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1931. After the museum relocated uptown, the nascent New York Studio School (NYSS) moved into the compound in 1967.

Over the past century Edward Hopper sketched, John Cage lectured and Philip Guston taught within these walls. Countless other greats practised, exhibited or, in the case of Marianne Faithfull, lived in what is now a National Historic Landmark. “This building has been the incubator for American art for 120 years,” says the artist Matthew Ritchie, sitting in a bare-bones conference room on a warm September afternoon. It has also been sorely in need of a makeover at least since he was a student here in the 1990s.
Leaks and hazards

When Ritchie was named the school’s director last year, the roof and studio skylights—coveted by students for their diffused natural light—leaked, the nearly century-old cloth-wrapped wiring had deteriorated dangerously and wheelchair access was extremely limited. His priority was renovation. The first phase—including doubling the public exhibition space and creating a new accessible lecture and performance hall in wood with stepped seating—is set to be completed this autumn, and phase two will begin in the spring.

Prior to Ritchie’s arrival, the school had obtained public grants for the necessary work, but they required matching funds and their expiration date was fast approaching. He quickly marshalled forces. The board agreed to donate the required money, he says, and the school tapped Matthew Baird of Baird Architects to helm the overhaul.

Ritchie and Baird’s history of collaboration dates back 17 years and across two other local institutions. In 2009, they teamed up to consider the effects of rising sea levels on the built environment as part of the interdisciplinary Rising Currents project at the Museum of Modern Art. Just a few years later, they put their theories into practice after Hurricane Sandy tore through the city, its storm surge flooding much of downtown. Ritchie was on the board of the beloved alternative art space The Kitchen when it enlisted Baird to rehabilitate its waterlogged lobby and black-box theatre.

The architect’s sensitive execution on that project—he preserved visual evidence of flood damage, for example—made him an obvious choice for the NYSS project, which presented a similar challenge. “You have this really cool building that’s got this patina of great artists that have moved through it,” Baird says. “How do you not erase that?”
Buried treasure

Thanks to Baird and Ritchie’s handle-with-care edict, the construction crew was on the lookout for treasures buried beneath layers of plasterboard. The artist Cecily Brown had told Ritchie that she painted her first mural on a school wall when she was a student in the 1990s but could not remember where. And the school archives held numerous photos of murals Whitney had commissioned from the artist Robert E. Locher for the original carriage house.

Sure enough, the crew uncovered the work of both artists within a 24-hour period. Brown’s piece—featuring disembodied penises, two of them appearing to kiss—is in the newly expanded gallery space on the main floor. To prevent it from potentially distracting from exhibitions, the design team installed a shallow cabinet in front of the mural.

Ritchie jokes that the set-up resembles a gabinetto segreto, or secret room, the most famous of which was a locked vault of erotic artefacts from Pompeii and Herculaneum. “Who doesn’t want a Cecily Brown mural? And then, who doesn’t want pornography in your brand-new public gallery?” he says with a laugh. “It’s the perfect combination.”

Workers discovered the two Locher murals where a bathroom and a hallway leading to it will be built. Intended to be viewed in the candlelight of Whitney’s dining room, one is a glimmering green, the other a trompe l’oeil image of doric columns. Baird tweaked the layout but not the location of the restroom. “Now it will be the most historic bathroom in New York,” Ritchie says.

A less fortuitous surprise: the beams beneath Robert Winthrop Chanler’s flame-motif fireplace in Whitney’s original second-floor studio were cracking, requiring emergency shoring up to stop the ceiling from collapse—together with the priceless fireplace. “This is the urgency of renovation,” Ritchie says. “You can wait too long, and then you lose it all.”
Super-tight deadlines

Because of the grant deadlines for the first phase of the project, Baird needed to work at warp speed, condensing three years of planning, permitting, bidding and execution into one. Owing to New York City’s complex building code, he approached the $2.2m renovation as “100 small projects” rather than gutting the 59,000 sq. ft building. The landmark-restoration specialist Jonathan Raible is overseeing the new roof.

In addition to enhancing the first floor’s public spaces, Baird rewired the building, renovated the wreck of a kitchen and improved accessibility by adding a wheelchair lift to the performance hall. “You can’t have a public programme if you don’t provide correct facilities for the public,” Ritchie says. “You’re not really welcoming them.”

Climbing the narrow staircases to the maze of studios where the school’s 27 full-time, in-person students work, Baird speaks enthusiastically about the second phase of renovations, which will include a student coffee bar. In keeping with his preservationist instincts, he plans to relamp with LED bulbs the elegant Fresnel recessed box lighting that Whitney installed for evenly washed walls, and he hopes to restore the system of baffles that modulated direct light in the studios as well as undertake other restoration while safeguarding the landmark’s character.

Ritchie already has his eye on another, likely longer-term fix for the school: free tuition. “That would require a very large endowment from extremely generous single or multiple donors,” he says, giving his best impression of a silver-tongued salesman, “which we’re eagerly awaiting with an entirely unique naming opportunity.”

absaetze.t: « Fassianos, ô Fassianos ! Je me souviens des premiers jours, quand me commença la surprise, d’une nouvelle façon d’aimer… » L’un compte parmi les plus grands auteurs français du XXe siècle, l’autre est considéré dans son pays natal comme le « Picasso grec ». À Paris, une exposition gratuite retrace, jusqu’au 12 décembre, la belle histoire d’amitié qui s’est écrite en mots et en images entre le peintre Alekos Fassianós (1935–2022) et Louis Aragon (1897–1982), quelques années seulement avant la disparition de ce dernier.

À la fin des années 1970, le vieux poète, que la mort a séparé d’Elsa, vit toujours dans leur appartement du 56 rue de Varenne, peuplé d’œuvres d’art et de souvenirs du couple. C’est là qu’il fait la rencontre du jeune peintre, qui n’a pas encore acquis la reconnaissance dont il jouira par la suite. Formé à l’École des beaux-arts d’Athènes dans l’atelier de Yánnis Móralis, Fassianós s’est installé à Paris en 1967 pour fuir la dictature des colonels.
Une même fascination pour l’amour et la mythologie

Depuis, il mène une carrière à rebours des canons de son temps. À l’heure où la tendance est à l’abstraction, il défend une peinture figurative et solaire, imprégnée des mythes et des couleurs de la Méditerranée. Cet artiste prolifique ne se limite d’ailleurs pas à la peinture puisqu’il est aussi écrivain, céramiste, designer, scénographe et architecte.

De ce véritable coup de foudre amical naît une relation de profonde estime à laquelle prend également part le poète d’origine iranienne Hamid Fouladvind (né en 1947). Collectionneur des œuvres de Fassianós avant même leur rencontre, Aragon lui consacre un texte très personnel, « Images chantées », qui vient clore ses Écrits sur l’art moderne et donne son titre à l’exposition.

Orchestrée par la curatrice Marion Gardair et présentée en collaboration avec le musée Fassianós d’Athènes et la Maison Triolet-Aragon, celle-ci réunit une dizaine d’œuvres et de précieux documents d’archives – lettres, dessins… Autant de témoignages qui révèlent comment les univers de ces deux artistes, décidément faits pour se rencontrer, se répondent autour d’une fascination commune pour l’amour et, bien sûr, la mythologie.
Des toiles comme surgies d’un rêve

Au-delà de cette amitié fertile, qui a donné lieu à de remarquables collaborations autour de livres, l’exposition met en lumière l’œuvre de Fassianós. Si le peintre est une véritable icône dans son pays, où un musée lui est consacré à Athènes, il demeure beaucoup moins connu en France.

Dans ses tableaux, les dieux de l’Antiquité côtoient des silhouettes anonymes alanguies, d’improbables cyclistes ou de beaux jeunes éphèbes. Ses visions aux couleurs éblouissantes, parfois rehaussées d’or, semblent surgir d’un rêve où les paysages et les intérieurs méditerranéens fusionnent avec l’urbanisme fonctionnel de la place d’Italie, aux abords de laquelle l’artiste avait installé son atelier. Un rêve éveillé où l’art et la poésie apparaissent comme l’un des plus beaux ciments de l’amitié.
